title: Deterministic QKD source robust against side-channel attacks
authors: Kiyoshi Tamaki, Marcos Curty, Akihiro Mizutani, Álvaro Navarrete
abstract: Quantum key distribution (QKD) is secure in principle, but practical security can be undermined by discrepancies between real devices and the idealized models assumed in security proofs. Source side channels, including those exploited by Trojan-horse attacks, are particularly detrimental: neglecting them compromises implementation security, whereas accounting for them reduces performance. Here we propose a QKD source that is intrinsically robust against side-channel attacks. Unlike existing passive and modulator-free schemes, it requires neither post-selection of the emitted pulses nor devices with a perfect extinction ratio to suppress side channels, and it does not introduce correlations between the intensity and the encoded bit or basis. Consequently, simpler security proofs apply directly, yielding substantially higher key rates. Our proposal appears to be within reach of current technology and therefore provides a clear and practical path toward implementation-secure QKD.
summary: This paper introduces a novel Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) source designed to be inherently secure against side-channel attacks like Trojan-horse attacks. By engineering the phase randomization across two stages, it achieves high key rates while eliminating reliance on imperfect components or post-selection procedures. This offers a practical path toward deploying truly implementation-secure quantum communication systems.
main_problem: Practical Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) security is threatened by source side channels, such as Trojan-horse attacks, which are not accounted for in idealized security proofs.
main_result: The authors propose a QKD source design that is intrinsically robust against these side-channel attacks without sacrificing key rate or requiring perfect components.
method: The scheme utilizes a two-stage process involving phase randomization and controlled phase shifts to ensure the output state's security relies on random phases unknown to an eavesdropper (Eve).
model_or_system: The system involves an Intensity Package (IntP) stage using gain-switched lasers, relative-phase measurement (RPM), and a phase modulator, followed by a second interference stage before single-photon attenuation.
key_observables: Output mean photon number ($\mu_{	ext{out}}$) and the resulting output phase ($	heta_{	ext{out}}$).
important_parameters: Phase shifts ($s_I, s_b$), path transmittances ($\eta_{path}, \eta$), and input mean photon numbers ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The security relies on five core assumptions (A1-A5), including stable intensities and the randomness of relative phases inaccessible to Eve.
figures_summary: Figure 1 shows the IntP stage components (HBS, RPM, PM); Figure 2 details the second stage involving interference and phase shifting before the quantum channel output.
paper_structure: The paper first identifies the security gap due to side channels. It then proposes the two-stage source architecture, detailing the physics of phase randomization in the IntP, followed by the basis-dependent encoding in the second stage to achieve optical privacy and high key rates.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses practical implementation loopholes in quantum communication protocols, which is a major focus area at the intersection of quantum optics and information theory.
